items.prompt: A TypeError is thrown while one comment in the comments panel is rendering. Which of the app's error layers handles it?
items.answer: The error boundary that wraps the comments section
distractors: The axios response interceptor in api-client.ts
react-query, which sets isError on the comments query
Sentry, which restores the panel after reporting it
items.explanation: Render errors are caught by the nearest React error boundary. discussion.tsx wraps <Comments> in its own ErrorBoundary, so that boundary catches it. Interceptors and isError handle failed requests, not render exceptions.

items.prompt: A click handler in a component throws synchronously. Which mechanism in the app catches it?
items.answer: None of the boundaries; wrap that handler in a try/catch
distractors: The nearest error boundary, which then shows its fallback
The app-wide boundary in provider.tsx, as the last resort
The response interceptor, which turns it into a toast
items.explanation: Error boundaries catch errors thrown during render and lifecycle methods only, not in event handlers or async code. The guide says to try/catch a handler that can throw.

items.prompt: Why does the error interceptor finish with return Promise.reject(error) instead of returning normally?
items.answer: So react-query still sees the failure and can set isError
distractors: So the toast is shown only after the caller has handled it
So that axios retries the request once before it gives up
So the 401 redirect runs before the toast has been added
items.explanation: Rejecting keeps the failure visible to callers: react-query marks the query errored and screens can react locally. Returning normally would turn every failure into a success with undefined data.

items.prompt: On a discussion page, the Comments component crashes during render. What does the user see?
items.answer: The discussion, with a scoped Failed to load comments message
distractors: A full-page MainErrorFallback that replaces the whole app
A blank white screen, since the crash unmounts the root
An error toast, while the comments show their last data
items.explanation: The route renders DiscussionView outside the comments boundary and <Comments> inside an ErrorBoundary whose fallback is "Failed to load comments. Try to refresh the page." Only that section is replaced.

items.prompt: When the server keeps the session in an HttpOnly cookie, what is left for this client to do?
items.answer: Set withCredentials so the cookie is sent with each request
distractors: Read the cookie in JS and copy it into an Authorization header
Keep a copy of the token in localStorage for page refreshes
Sign each request with the cookie value by using js-cookie
items.explanation: JavaScript cannot read an HttpOnly cookie at all, so the client only has to let it ride along: authRequestInterceptor sets config.withCredentials = true on every request.

items.prompt: Discussion bodies are user-written markdown rendered as HTML. What stops an injected script tag from running?
items.answer: DOMPurify sanitizes the parsed HTML before it is injected
distractors: React escapes it, as it escapes any string it renders
The mock server strips HTML tags before saving a body
A Content-Security-Policy meta tag set in index.html
items.explanation: MDPreview passes DOMPurify.sanitize(parse(value)) to dangerouslySetInnerHTML. That prop bypasses React's escaping, which is why sanitizing first is required.

items.prompt: Which mechanism decides whether a USER may delete one particular comment?
items.answer: A policy function comparing the comment author with the user
distractors: A role check that sets allowedRoles to the USER role alone
A server lookup run inside the Authorization component
A permission flag that the API stores on each comment
items.explanation: The rule depends on the resource, so it is PBAC: POLICIES["comment:delete"] returns true for ADMIN or when comment.author?.id === user.id, and comments-list passes the result as policyCheck.

items.prompt: A button is wrapped in <Authorization allowedRoles={[]}>. Which signed-in users see it?
items.answer: Every signed-in user, since an empty list grants access
distractors: Nobody, since no role appears in the empty roles list
Only admins, since ADMIN is the default allowed role
Nobody, since TypeScript rejects an empty roles array
items.explanation: checkAccess only filters when allowedRoles.length > 0; otherwise it returns true. RoleTypes[] accepts an empty array, so it compiles and renders the children for anyone.

items.prompt: A developer passes both allowedRoles and policyCheck to the Authorization component. What happens?
items.answer: TypeScript rejects it, because the props form a union
distractors: It compiles, and access then needs both checks to pass
It compiles, and allowedRoles wins over policyCheck
It compiles, and whichever prop comes first is used
items.explanation: AuthorizationProps is a discriminated union: one branch has allowedRoles with policyCheck?: never, the other policyCheck with allowedRoles?: never. Passing both matches neither branch, so the call does not type-check.

items.prompt: A component calls useAuthorization() while no user is logged in. What does the hook do?
items.answer: It throws an Error with the message User does not exist!
distractors: It returns a checkAccess function that always gives false
It returns role undefined and a checkAccess that is true
It redirects the browser to the login page by itself
items.explanation: useAuthorization reads useUser() and, if user.data is missing, throws Error("User does not exist!"). It never returns or redirects in that case.

items.prompt: According to the testing chapter, which kind of test should most of this app's tests be?
items.answer: Integration tests that render a route against MSW
distractors: Unit tests for every component, kept in isolation
End-to-end Playwright tests covering every flow
Snapshot tests that pin the markup of each page
items.explanation: Integration tests render a feature with the real router, react-query and forms, with MSW as the far end. Unit tests are for shared or complex pieces and e2e tests stay few, on money paths.

items.prompt: Why does the testing chapter prefer MSW to mocking the fetch function in integration tests?
items.answer: Requests still pass through the real API client and its interceptors
distractors: MSW speeds tests up by skipping all JSON serialization of request bodies
MSW records responses from the real server and replays them later on
A mocked fetch cannot return a JSON body when tests run under Vitest
items.explanation: MSW intercepts real HTTP requests, so the component, hook, api client and interceptors all run; only the server is fake. Mocking fetch skips the API layer entirely.

items.front: Name the three error-handling layers and what each catches.
items.back: API: the axios response interceptor handles failed HTTP requests (toast, 401 redirect, reject). UI: React error boundaries, app-wide and per-section, catch exceptions thrown during render. Production: an error tracking service such as Sentry catches everything after shipping.

items.front: Compare storing a session token in localStorage with an HttpOnly cookie.
items.back: localStorage: simple, but any XSS can read and steal the token. HttpOnly cookie: JavaScript cannot read it, so XSS cannot steal it; the risk becomes CSRF, mitigated by SameSite and CSRF tokens. The client then only needs withCredentials = true.

items.front: What is Testing Library's core rule, and which habits follow from it?
items.back: Test what the user experiences, not the implementation: implementation-coupled tests fail on harmless refactors and pass on broken UI. Prefer getByRole/getByLabelText, use findBy* for async content, and userEvent over fireEvent.

items.front: What three purposes does the MSW mock backend serve in this repo?
items.back: Development without a backend, integration tests that send real requests through the real API client, and API design: the handlers (business logic over an in-memory db) act as an executable spec. MSW does not run in production.
